say: Class chat is open. The question: which business would you actually launch this term? Pitch it with a payer, a price in euros, a first test and the loop that runs without you.

At my hotel I answer the same five questions in four languages every night. I’d try a QR guest helper for small Riga hotels: €25 a month, guests pay nothing. Wi-Fi passwords should not need a night shift.

My dad’s workshop loses customers when he’s under a tractor and can’t answer the phone. I’d try an enquiry helper for small repair shops outside Riga—not automatic quotes, just getting customers a reply and the owner a usable job request.

Let me push back: selling fear of fines without legal expertise is a liability, not a business. In my research work, chasing documents eats more time than interpreting rules. I'd test certificate-expiry tracking with Riga construction subcontractors bidding for tenders: €35 a month, but only if missed paperwork has actually cost them work.
Elīna, I back I2: you can reach the first owner tonight, and from building a volunteer bot I know collecting missing details is something we can ship this week.

Dominykas, who actually approves the €35—the owner or whoever prepares tenders? At our carpentry shop my mother handles paperwork, but my father approves spending; which ten subcontractors would you call this week, and how would you reach the person who can say yes?

Elīna, from my call-centre experience, we should check whether customers finish the questions before building the helper. Your dad could send a free form to his next five callers; compare how many follow-up calls he needs with his usual jobs.

test: This week, ask my dad and two other owners to share a mobile enquiry page with customers; spend under €20 and measure completed requests and owner time saved over seven days.
Within two days, have Elīna’s dad send a free mobile form asking for machine model, fault, photo and callback number to his next five callers; manually organise replies and record completion,…

say: Dominykas, in my research job, people agreeing to try something is not evidence they’ll pay. Let’s test I3 without building anything: manually track documents and ask for an actual €10 payment, not a hypothetical yes.

test: Call ten subcontractors this week; get two to trial tracking five non-sensitive certificates each, spending under €30, and ask whether either would pay €35 for continued tracking.
Within three days, call ten Riga subcontractors and offer manual tracking of five non-sensitive certificates for €10 for one week. Use a free spreadsheet and email reminders; spend €0, count actual…

say: Elīna, on our farm a broken tractor means we phone the next workshop if nobody answers. Does your dad miss calls entirely, or mainly waste time collecting details? If it’s missed calls, the form needs to go out automatically after one, otherwise we’re fixing the wrong problem.

Elīna, I can build the form tomorrow, but automatic missed-call SMS depends on your dad’s phone setup—not just an n8n flow. From my website gigs, getting owners to change their routine is harder than shipping the page. What phone does he use, and would he actually send callers the link?

Dominykas, at our carpentry shop my mother keeps document dates in a spreadsheet; chasing replacements takes longer than spotting expiry dates. I3 earns its €35 only if it follows up with whoever supplies the replacement, not just sends her another reminder. Ask the first owner to show us that chase.

Nikita, in my fintech interviews, people saying “useful” often meant “I wouldn’t use it.” Before the QR page, can we sit through one reception shift and count which questions guests ask despite existing signs? That tells us whether I1 needs better answers or whether guests just want a person.

Nikita, at my parents’ guesthouse the easy questions repeat, but late check-in and room changes still need us. Does I1 run from approved answers without us checking every conversation, and who at the property handles uncertain requests after reception closes? That boundary matters more than adding languages.
I back I3: missing tender paperwork can cost actual revenue. €35 works for a Riga pilot; Nordic expansion needs proof it saves administrator hours.
mārtiņš, some android phones can automate missed-call texts, but permissions need testing on his actual phone. iphone is trickier. apparently even tractors need a compatibility check.
Nikita, guests may enter booking numbers or passport details even if we only ask about Wi-Fi. Can we warn them and avoid storing conversations?
My mum writes bookings in a notebook after closing. For I2, show the owner can use requests without copying everything into another system; then I’d back it.

Gabrielė, yes, count one shift first. Laura, unresolved questions go to the existing on-call contact, not an imaginary night receptionist. Līga, let’s start with FAQ buttons, no free text or stored conversations; Wi-Fi doesn’t need your passport.

test: Visit five properties this week; get one owner's approved FAQ and test a QR page with guests for seven days, spending under €30 and counting questions resolved without reception.
Count questions during one shift; trial approved FAQ buttons at one property for seven days, under €30; compare reception questions.
loop: AI answers from the hotel's approved information in Latvian, Russian, English and German; uncertain questions go to reception, and a hotel staff member approves information changes and checks flagged answers weekly.
AI translates approved FAQs; buttons display answers and on-call contact; no free text or conversation storage; staff approve changes.

say: Kristaps, the owner approves spending; the administrator shows us the chase. Maarja, agreed on actual €10 payment: let me push back on counting free trials as demand.

test: Within three days, call ten Riga subcontractors and offer manual tracking of five non-sensitive certificates for €10 for one week. Use a free spreadsheet and email reminders; spend €0, count actual…
Call ten Riga subcontractors; ask owners for €10 paid pilots and administrators to demonstrate replacement chasing; spend €0.

say: Nikita, who checks the Latvian translations before guests see them? I can check German, but staff should approve practical details like check-in instructions.
Dāvis, missed calls are the pain; Mārtiņš, I’ll check Dad’s phone before promising automation. Which workshop owners beyond Dad would actually pay €20, and how do we reach ten this week?
Elīna, send me his phone model. I’ll test missed-call SMS tomorrow; I back I2 if callers complete the form without Dad chasing them.
Empty shelves lose customers; extra yoghurt becomes family dinner. I’d test order drafts in my parents’ shops, not sell grocers another dashboard.
Elīna, I can ask our cooperative’s machinery contact for workshop introductions tomorrow. I’ll back it when missed-call texts bring completed requests without your dad chasing.
My parents’ Sigulda tours get winter enquiries that never become bookings. I’d test an enquiry follow-up service, charging only for completed bookings, not another monthly subscription.
Nordic buyers send our Kaunas factory questionnaires that eat export-team hours. I’d sell evidence-linked drafts, not invented certificates, and test through Dad’s export contacts.
Nikita, that answers my concern. I back I1: approved FAQs and an existing on-call contact keep exceptions with staff. Can we secure one owner’s permission tomorrow?
I back I6: export staff already spend hours on these questionnaires. Lukas, measure review time too, so we know drafts actually save work.
Madara, what counts as a booking we actually won? A friendly reminder feels useful ✨ but 5% on someone already coming could upset owners.
Mārtiņš, I’ll get the phone model tomorrow; Dāvis, introductions would help. Repeated missed calls shouldn’t trigger repeated texts: that could annoy customers before Dad even speaks to them.
I back I6: reusable, evidence-linked answers make this a real loop. I can build document matching tonight; unsupported answers stay blank for staff.
Madara, could we split comparable enquiries into follow-up and no-follow-up groups this week? That would test whether reminders add bookings before we promise owners a commission model.
Leon, agreed. In Kaunas we’ll time drafting plus staff review against their last questionnaire; faster drafting means nothing if checking takes longer.

test: Contact five exporters; draft one redacted questionnaire each; seek one €25 paid pilot within seven days; spend €20.
Five Kaunas exporters; compare drafting plus review against previous questionnaire; seek one €25 pilot within seven days; spend €20.

say: Rokas, bread leftovers and Saturday bun shortages are exactly our bakery problem 🥐. Can imports run without us, with owners only checking flagged quantities?
Start smaller. Three FAQ buttons at one hostel tomorrow. If guests still ask reception the same questions, another screen solves nothing.

test: Count questions during one shift; trial approved FAQ buttons at one property for seven days, under €30; compare reception questions.
Tomorrow test three approved FAQ buttons with ten arriving guests at one hostel. Free page; count reception questions avoided.

say: Elīna, MVP: one text per number per day, no repeat spam. Three of five callers completing requests without chasing would convince me to back I2.
Mārtiņš, agreed, but texts cost money even when nobody completes the form. Let’s count SMS costs too; they must fit inside €20 a month.
Elīna, SMS cost matters, but language could kill completion first. Let callers choose Latvian or Russian; a half-understood repair form saves nobody time.
Sanita, can your till email stock files daily without us? Imports and drafts can run nightly; owners still check actual stock and approve orders. Squashed buns fool spreadsheets 🛒.
I back I3: the €10 paid pilot tests demand without building software. Count payments received, not owners who agree to pay later.
Madara, Mum pays me €30 a month for salon Instagram. Would tour owners prefer €25 monthly over losing 5% of every booking? ✨
Lukas, how many questionnaires arrive monthly? One per quarter makes €100 monthly hard to retain. A paid pilot plus repeat volume would convince me.
Edgars, agreed. Latvian and Russian, checked by Dad before sending. Let’s make photos optional too; uploading one shouldn’t stop a callback request.
Rokas, warehouse stock files can describe imaginary vegetables 😅. Show imports run unattended and drafts save time after owners check actual stock, then I’m in.
Elīna, I’ll log SMS spend alongside completions. MVP passes if three of five callers finish without chasing and projected SMS costs leave margin at €20.
Artūrs, fair. I’ll check frequency with the Kaunas exporters; €50 per questionnaire makes more sense until repeat volume justifies monthly billing.
Elīna, shared workshop phones are a data risk. MVP needs a private owner inbox, not a public spreadsheet full of callback numbers.
I back I1: arriving tired in a new country, finding the Wi-Fi and late check-in instructions in your language is a small rescue.
Roberts, agreed. Three mornings, one shop, bread only. Count checking time too; imaginary carrots can sit this one out 🛒.

test: Run seven days of order drafts at parents’ two shops; compare owner corrections and ordering time; spend under €20.
Three mornings, parents’ shop: unattended bread-stock imports; compare drafting plus owner checks against usual ordering time; spend €0.

say: I back I6: evidence-linked drafts tackle paid staff time, not imaginary fear of fines. Let me push back on scope: missing evidence must stay missing.
🎧 I5 could sell, but who gets credit when a customer replies by phone? Show me booking attribution without making the operator do extra admin.
i back i6. helpdesk staff cost €1,200 a month; €50 needs real hours saved. lukas, does that price survive review time, or just typing time?

Anete, would €25 monthly really sell when some winter weeks bring no bookings? For my parents’ tours, 5% on a €100 booking is €5, with nothing owed in empty weeks. But we should charge only for recovered enquiries, not every booking.
Rokas, I back this test. €30 is reasonable if checking plus drafting beats normal ordering. If not, we’ve built a bun spreadsheet with opinions 😅.
I back I2. Dad loses repair jobs while he’s under a car; capturing the request before the caller tries another workshop is worth testing.
Roberts, faster ordering still fails if we run out by lunch. I’ll log leftover bread and stockouts too; stopwatch wins don’t feed customers 🛒.
Lukas, can incoming questionnaires reach the drafting step without us uploading them? Who checks source documents are current before export staff approve answers?
Lukas, I can ask exporters in the coworking network how questionnaires arrive. Email attachments versus buyer portals could mean very different amounts of manual work.
I3: issue date plus one year is not an expiry date. Require administrator confirmation before reminders start, or we automate very punctual nonsense.
Mārtiņš, private inbox agreed. But customer photos can show faces or number plates; let’s ask for machine-only photos and delete pilot requests after testing.
A QR code beside reception misses the tired guest outside a locked door. Nikita, can the hostel include the link in its pre-arrival message?
During my Stockholm bank internship, chasing supporting documents took longer than drafting answers. I back I6: measure the evidence hunt too, not just typing.
Aino, email attachments can enter the drafting queue automatically through a dedicated inbox. Buyer portals stay manual for the pilot; export staff must confirm source documents are current.

Toms, €50 has to beat total staff time, including evidence hunting and review, not typing. Leon, ask the Kaunas contacts about email versus portals before we promise automation. Aino, staff must approve document versions first; otherwise we’re selling faster mistakes.

Hanna, yes, include the link in pre-arrival messages, but keep door codes off the public page. Will owners actually pay €25 after the free month? That’s seven €3.50 coffees for me; let’s ask before building.
I back I6 because unsupported claims stay unsupported. Does the inbox-to-draft loop run without us, with export staff checking sources and approving EVERY answer?
My agency automation benchmark is €200–500/month. Does I6’s €50 cover setup too? Let’s time document onboarding separately before promising that price.
I6 is closest for me. Faster test: sell one €25 manual draft before coding; include onboarding and review time. A payment beats ten people saying “useful.

test: Five Kaunas exporters; compare drafting plus review against previous questionnaire; seek one €25 pilot within seven days; spend €20.
Call ten exporters; sell one €25 draft before coding; time onboarding, drafting and review on one redacted questionnaire; €0.

say: Elīna, agreed. Machine-only photos, private inbox, delete after pilot. I back I2: we can ship this MVP tomorrow and measure actual completed enquiries.
Lukas, at the Hamburg port internship, buyer portals meant manual copying. I’ll ask my coworking contacts for exporter introductions and check intake before promising automation.
Mārtiņš, yes. But five completed forms aren't five saved jobs. Dad should log callback time and whether each enquiry becomes a repair.
On a €100 tour booking, our 5% earns €5. Does that cover checking replies and matching phone bookings, or should I5 start with email-only enquiries?
I6: truck paperwork taught me one wrong delivery address can cost more than the fee. Who checks scanned tables haven't shifted answers into the wrong rows?
🎧 Madara, email-only first. Ten winter enquiries could produce zero bookings just from seasonality; show one recovered booking and minutes spent checking before I back.
Rokas, parents are forgiving customers 😅. Ask one nearby owner to pay €30 after seeing the three-morning results. Otherwise we’ve proved family support, not demand.
Madara, start with five recent unanswered email quotes tomorrow ✨ No chasing phone bookings yet. Log replies, confirmed bookings and checking minutes.

test: This week, follow up ten consented winter enquiries at parents’ company; spend €0, count completed bookings.
Tomorrow, manually follow up five consented unanswered email quotes; log replies, confirmed bookings and checking minutes over seven days; €0.

say: Elīna, agreed. Building three local business websites taught me that a working form isn't proof of sales. MVP log: completed enquiry, callback minutes, confirmed repair.
Paulius, agreed, but a confirmed booking can still cancel. I’ll match email replies to completed tours; zero bookings means no commission, not proven demand.

test: Tomorrow, manually follow up five consented unanswered email quotes; log replies, confirmed bookings and checking minutes over seven days; €0.
Tomorrow follow up five consented unanswered email quotes; log replies, cancellations, completed tours and checking minutes for seven days; €0.

say: Roberts, fair. Mum pays me in dinner 😅 I’ll show one nearby owner the results and ask for €30 for the next month.
I back I6: sourced drafts solve real paperwork. But €50 disappears quickly if every questionnaire needs fresh document cleanup; time that separately.
Mārtiņš, yes. Let’s ask two unrelated workshop owners to try it too; Dad’s patience with us isn’t proof someone will pay €20.
Ten guests opening I1 isn’t ten questions avoided. Let’s count repeat questions per occupied room against a normal shift. Clicks don’t let me sleep.

test: Tomorrow test three approved FAQ buttons with ten arriving guests at one hostel. Free page; count reception questions avoided.
One hostel, seven days: compare repeat questions per occupied room against baseline; ask owner for €25 continuation; spend €0.

say: I1 who updates changed breakfast times and broken links? Does anything run without us after setup or are we selling a page with ongoing maintenance?
🎧 Madara, fair, completed tours count. Who pays the 5% exactly, owner or booking manager, and how do we reach ten operators beyond your parents’ partners?
Let me push back: ten calls aren't the test. For I3, sell one €10 manual pilot tomorrow before building extraction; a calendar can test the pain.

test: Call ten Riga subcontractors; ask owners for €10 paid pilots and administrators to demonstrate replacement chasing; spend €0.
Tomorrow call three subcontractors; sell one €10 pilot tracking five certificates with calendar reminders; measure administrator time saved; €0.

say: I back I4 🥐. Track unsold bread and missed bun sales too; faster ordering means little if we still order the wrong quantities.
I back I6. For the paid pilot, ask for a second questionnaire at €50 after delivery. That tests repeat demand, not just curiosity.
Paulius, the operator’s owner pays from completed tour revenue. I’ll contact ten independent Sigulda operators through public business emails this week, asking owners about unanswered winter quotes.
